subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the module structure using the SDK's part and joint helpers, being cautious since I can't verify the exact API—planning a root "base" joint plus a "lidHinge" joint for the lid, with THREE geometries for the parts since that's the safest approach.

For the lid, I'm baking rotations directly into the geometry rather than relying on uncertain part options: building the lid shape in a local frame relative to the hinge (closed state extending forward), then rotating it about the X axis to simulate the lid swinging open roughly 110 degrees backward.

I'm defining the chest dimensions now—body as a box roughly 0.9 wide, 0.55 deep, 0.4 tall, with the hinge placed at the back top edge—and starting to construct the lid as a half-cylinder arch using those measurements.

Setting chest depth to 0.55 with radius 0.275, I'm adding end caps using half-circle geometry oriented to face outward at the chest's sides, plus thin half-cylinder wood panels and slightly larger strap bands positioned along the lid for reinforcement detail.

Now I'm building the main body as a 0.9x0.4x0.55 box with darker plank lines, iron corner bands, vertical straps with studs, and separate interior walls to hold a mound of spilled gold coins and flattened sphere treasure near the open top.

I'll scatter coin cylinders with random tilts using my own deterministic random generator rather than relying on an uncertain external rng function. For the lid's underside, I need to add an inner lining shell so the interior isn't left looking hollow and open.

Actually, a cleaner approach is to build the lid as an extruded arch shape with outer and inner arcs, giving it real thickness so both the wood exterior and velvet-lined interior read correctly from any viewing angle.

Adding iron straps and plank seam details to the lid using thin arch shapes, positioning them along the x-axis with darker tones for visual texture.

For the lid helper, I'll rotate the geometry negatively by the open angle and translate it to the hinge position before building the part with its bone joint, assuming the SDK handles local positioning via the bone itself. Now I'm moving on to the lock/hasp with a padlock element.

I need to position a small lid hasp plate, then place the carved skull on the front plank offset to the left of center so the hanging padlock doesn't fully cover it, keeping both within the strap boundaries.

For the skull itself, I'm building it from a flattened pale bone-colored sphere for the cranium, a small jaw box, dark sunken eye socket spheres, and crossed bone boxes beneath, using a dim bone color to give it a carved, inlaid look rather than a glossy one.

Now I'm working out a draped pearl necklace -- a curve of small pearl spheres arcing from a mound near the top, over the front rim edge, and spilling down to coil loosely on the floor.

I'm repositioning the necklace to the right side of the composition, around x=0.35, so it clears the skull and the lock and sits just past the strap without overlapping them, while sketching out the manual point path for the drape over the rim and down the outside wall.

I'll let it pool on the floor with a gentle curve inward, then build it as a Catmull-Rom curve sampled into 30 evenly spaced points for the pearls at a small radius, plus a gold clasp. For the goblet, I'm thinking of placing it tilted on the mound near the front-left and constructing it as a lathe geometry with a profile defining the base, stem, and cup.

Scattering red and green gem shapes across the mound and floor, then placing around 60 coins over the mound surface with random tilts, plus another 25 spilling onto the floor in a fan pattern and a small stack nearby, cycling through a few gold color variants for variety. I'm also adding a stream of coins spilling over the front rim to make the pile feel dynamic.

I'm defining the coin geometry as small cylinders rotated and translated individually across the scatter positions, keeping the part count reasonable. For the chest body itself, I'm building the front, back, and sides out of separate plank boxes with slightly varied brown tones to suggest hand-weathered wood, plus a floor panel to complete the structure.

Now I'm adding thin red lining boxes just inside the walls to simulate interior fabric, along with small wooden feet blocks at the corners so the chest sits slightly raised off the floor. I'm double-checking the vertical placement so the floor box, feet, and coins all align properly at y≈0 without clipping through the ground.

Then I'm detailing the iron hardware: corner brackets as vertical boxes at each edge, horizontal metal bands across the front and back, and vertical straps with small rounded studs rendered as low-poly spheres, all colored with rusty brown-iron tones.

For the lid I'm adding hinge barrels at the back using thin cylinders, plus matching strap and stud details on the lid itself, translating the arch strap geometry to align with the lid's corners and adding a final iron rim band near the lid edges.

I'm working out the arch extrusion math: extruding along one axis then rotating so the shape spans correctly across the lid's depth, with the hinge positioned at the back wall and the lid half-depth set to match the body, then setting the lid's open angle to 105 degrees.

Computing the rotated coordinates confirms the lid swings up and slightly back, with the arch bulge curving outward toward the back and the top of the lid landing around y≈0.93, which looks right.

For the hinge joint setup, I'm translating the lid's z-offset by the radius after rotation so the arch spans from the hinge to twice the radius, keeping it centered correctly. Setting up hinge joints...

Now I'm working out the lid's inner lining geometry and surface details—adding a thinner arch for the lining inset from the outer wood shell, then defining a helper to compute local positions along the lid's curved surface for placing studs and seam boxes at specific angles and radii.

Writing more geometry helpers and setting up the skull decoration's position and scaled cranium sphere on the front plank face...

Still designing the padlock...

For the goblet, I'm defining a lathe profile with a lathe-generated geometry—base, stem, and an open cup shape—using a gold color for the material.

I'm placing gem decorations: small octahedra arranged around the cup's rim, plus a torus ring at the stem and a small sphere knob. For gem colors I'm using red and green, scattered across the mound and floor using icosahedron shapes.

For the coin mound I'm modeling it as an ellipsoid surface and sampling points on its upper half to position tilted coins with random rotation, using a flattened low-poly gold sphere as the base shape, while watching for coins clipping through the mound surface.

For the floor spill I'm scattering roughly 40 coins in a cluster region with random yaw and slight tilt, adding a small stacked pile of six coins, and leaning a few coins against the front rim wall with a steep tilt rotation.

Now I'm plotting a necklace draping over the mound surface, tracing pearl positions from the body up over the rim lip (keeping pearl centers above the rim top so they clear the plank edge) and down the front onto the floor, forming a loose strap that curves across the base without overlapping the corner pile.

I'm also scattering loose gems near the pile on the floor, roughly tallying the total part count (body, lid, coins, pearls, gems) to stay well under budget, and keeping the color palette compact — around 30 distinct colors for wood, metal, gems, and bone tones.

For procedural placement of coins and gems I'm setting up a small seeded pseudo-random number generator so the scatter looks natural but reproducible.

Now I'm defining the joint hierarchy API (root joint with no parent, children referencing a parent joint) and writing a function to extrude an arch shape — tracing the outer and inner radius as a 2D shape, extruding it along a length, then centering and rotating it into place along the correct axis.

Working out lid geometry next...

Still working out hinge barrel placement, then I'm adding a hasp plate at the lid's front edge, positioning the box geometry along the local tangent direction.
